listen_text: Section. Infinitesimals and Differentiation. Newton and Leibniz discovered the calculus (independently) at the end of the seventeenth century. A particularly important application of the calculus was differentiation. Roughly speaking, differentiation aims to give a notion of the “rate of change”, or gradient, of a function at a point. Here is a vivid way to illustrate the idea. Consider the function f of x equals x squared over four plus one half , depicted in black below: Coordinate diagram for the function f of x equals x squared over four plus one half. The horizontal axis is x , and the vertical axis is f of x . The horizontal tick labels use the horizontal-axis tick values one through four ; the vertical tick labels use the vertical-axis tick values one through five . A black upward-opening parabola is shown. Three right secant triangles share the point where x is one half. The red triangle has base three and slope one; the smaller blue triangle has base two and slope three quarters; the smallest green triangle has base one and slope one half. End diagram. Suppose we want to find the gradient of the function at c equals one half . We start by drawing a triangle whose hypotenuse approximates the gradient at that point, perhaps the red triangle above. When beta is the base length of our triangle, its height is f of one half plus beta, minus f of one half , so that the gradient of the hypotenuse is: Displayed expression. the quantity f of one half plus beta, minus f of one half, divided by beta. End displayed expression. So the gradient of our red triangle, with base length three , is exactly one . The hypotenuse of a smaller triangle, the blue triangle with base length two , gives a better approximation; its gradient is three quarters . A yet smaller triangle, the green triangle with base length one , gives a yet better approximation; with gradient one half . Ever-smaller triangles give us ever-better approximations. So we might say something like this: the hypotenuse of a triangle with an infinitesimal base length gives us the gradient at c equals one half itself. In this way, we would obtain a formula for the (first) derivative of the function f at the point c : Displayed expression. f prime of c equals the quantity f of c plus beta minus f of c, divided by beta, where beta is infinitesimal. End displayed expression. And, roughly, this is what Newton and Leibniz said. However, since they have said this, we must ask them: what is an infinitesimal? A serious dilemma arises. If beta equals zero , then f prime is ill-defined, for it involves dividing by zero . But if beta is greater than zero , then we just get an approximation to the gradient, and not the gradient itself. This is not an anachronistic concern. Here is Berkeley, criticizing Newton's followers: Quotation. I admit that signs may be made to denote either any thing or nothing: and consequently that in the original notation c plus beta , beta might have signified either an increment or nothing. But then which of these soever you make it signify, you must argue consistently with such its signification, and not proceed upon a double meaning: Which to do were a manifest sophism. ( George Berkeley's The Analyst , variables changed to match preceding text) End quotation. To defend the infinitesimal calculus against Berkeley, one might reply that the talk of “infinitesimals” is merely figurative. One might say that, so long as we take a really small triangle, we will get a good enough approximation to the tangent. Berkeley had a reply to this too: whilst that might be good enough for engineering, it undermines the status of mathematics, for Quotation. we are told that in rebus mathematicis errores quam minimi non sunt contemnendi. Translation. In the case of mathematics, the smallest errors are not to be neglected. End translation. George Berkeley's The Analyst End quotation. The italicised passage is a near-verbatim quote from Newton's own Quadrature of Curves (one thousand seven hundred four). Berkeley's philosophical objections are deeply incisive. Nevertheless, the calculus was a massively successful enterprise, and mathematicians continued to use it without falling into error. End section.

listen_text: Section. Rigorous Definition of Limits. These days, the standard solution to the foregoing problem is to get rid of the infinitesimals. Here is how. We saw that, as beta gets smaller, we get better approximations of the gradient. Indeed, as beta gets arbitrarily close to zero , the value of f prime of c “tends without limit” to the gradient we want. So, instead of considering what happens at beta equals zero , we need only consider the trend of f prime of c as beta approaches zero . Put like this, the general challenge is to make sense of claims of this shape: As x approaches c , g of x tends without limit to ell . which we can write more compactly as follows: Displayed expression. the limit, as x tends to c, of g of x equals ell. End displayed expression. In the nineteenth century, building upon earlier work by Cauchy, Weierstrass offered a perfectly rigorous definition of this expression. The idea is indeed that we can make g of x as close as we like to ell , by making x suitably close to c . More precisely, we stipulate that the limit, as x tends to c, of g of x equals ell will mean: Displayed expression. for every positive epsilon, there exists a positive delta such that, for every x, if the absolute value of x minus c is less than delta, then the absolute value of g of x minus ell is less than epsilon. End displayed expression. The vertical bars here indicate absolute magnitude. That is, the absolute value of x equals x when x is greater than or equal to zero , and the absolute value of x equals negative x when x is less than zero ; you can depict that function as follows: Coordinate diagram of the absolute-value function. The horizontal axis is x , and the vertical axis is the absolute value of x . The horizontal tick command uses the printed horizontal-axis tick values, including the duplicated positive-one position ; the vertical tick command uses the vertical-axis tick values one and two . The thick graph is a V shape, descending with slope negative one to the origin and ascending with slope one from the origin. The source tick list prints positive one twice; that duplication is preserved and disclosed. End diagram. So the definition says roughly this: you can make your “error” less than epsilon (that is, the absolute value of g of x minus ell is less than epsilon ) by choosing arguments which are no more than delta away from c (that is, the absolute value of x minus c is less than delta ). Source anomaly note. Source diagram note. The horizontal tick list prints the positive-one position twice, once as a bare value and once with an explicit label. The duplicate source command is retained; the graph itself remains the usual absolute-value V shape. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Having defined the notion of a limit, we can use it to avoid infinitesimals altogether, stipulating that the gradient of f at c is given by: Displayed expression. f prime of c equals the limit, as x tends to zero, of the quantity f of c plus x minus f of c, divided by x, where a limit exists. End displayed expression. It is important, though, to realise why our definition needs the caveat “where a limit exists”. To take a simple example, consider f of x equals the absolute value of x , whose graph we just saw. Evidently, f prime of zero is ill-defined: if we approach zero “from the right”, the gradient is always one ; if we approach zero “from the left”, the gradient is always negative one ; so the limit is undefined. As such, we might add that a function f is differentiable at x if and only if such a limit exists. We have seen how to handle differentiation using the notion of a limit. We can use the same notion to define the idea of a continuous function. (Bolzano had, in effect, realised this by one thousand eight hundred seventeen.) The Cauchy—Weierstrass treatment of continuity is as follows. Roughly: a function f is continuous (at a point) provided that, if you demand a certain amount of precision concerning the output of the function, you can guarantee this by insisting upon a certain amount of precision concerning the input of the function. More precisely: f is continuous at c provided that, as x tends to zero, the difference between f of c plus x and f of c itself tends to zero . Otherwise put: f is continuous at c if and only if f of c equals the limit, as x tends to c, of f of x . To go any further would just lead us off into real analysis, when our subject matter is set theory. So now we should pause, and state the moral. During the nineteenth century, mathematicians learnt how to do without infinitesimals, by invoking a rigorously defined notion of a limit. End section.

listen_text: Section. Pathologies. However, the definition of a limit turned out to allow for some rather “pathological” constructions. Around the eighteen thirties, Bolzano discovered a function which was continuous everywhere, but differentiable nowhere. (Unfortunately, Bolzano never published this; the idea was first encountered by mathematicians in one thousand eight hundred seventy two, thanks to Weierstrass's independent discovery of the same idea.) Footnote. The history is documented in extremely thorough footnotes to the Wikipedia article on the linked Wikipedia article on the Weierstrass function . End footnote. This was, to say the least, rather surprising. It is easy to find functions, such as the absolute value of x , which are continuous everywhere but not differentiable at a particular point. But a function which is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere is a very different beast. Consider, for a moment, how you might try to draw such a function. To ensure it is continuous, you must be able to draw it without ever removing your pen from the page; but to ensure it is differentiable nowhere, you would have to abruptly change the direction of your pen, constantly. Further “pathologies” followed. In January five one thousand eight hundred seventy four, Cantor wrote a letter to Dedekind, posing the problem: Quotation. Can a surface (say a square including its boundary) be one-to-one correlated to a line (say a straight line including its endpoints) so that to every point of the surface there corresponds a point of the line, and conversely to every point of the line there corresponds a point of the surface? It still seems to me at the moment that the answer to this question is very difficult—although here too one is so impelled to say no that one would like to hold the proof to be almost superfluous. Attribution. Quoted in Fernando Gouvea's account Was Cantor Surprised . End attribution. End quotation. But, in one thousand eight hundred seventy seven, Cantor proved that he had been wrong. In fact, a line and a square have exactly the same number of points. He wrote on twenty nine June one thousand eight hundred seventy seven to Dedekind “ je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas ”; that is, “I see it, but I don't believe it”. In the “received history” of mathematics, this is often taken to indicate just how literally incredible these new results were to the mathematicians of the time. (The correspondence is presented in Fernando Gouvea's account Was Cantor Surprised , and we return to it in the section More Myth than History . Cantor's proof is outlined in the section Cantor on the Line and the Plane .) Inspired by Cantor's result, Peano started to consider whether it might be possible to map a line smoothly onto a plane. This would be a curve which fills space. In eighteen ninety , Peano constructed just such a curve. This is truly counter-intuitive: Euclid had defined a line as “breadthless length” (Book I, Definition two), but Peano had shown that, by curling up a line appropriately, its length can be turned into breadth. In eighteen ninety-one , Hilbert described a slightly more intuitive space-filling curve, together with some pictures illustrating it. The curve is constructed in sequence, and here are the first six stages of the construction: Six square panels show the first six Hilbert-curve approximations in source order: stages one, two, and three across the top row, then stages four, five, and six across the bottom row. Each red curve lies in a gray square. The step sizes halve from stage to stage, while the recursive order rises from one through six, making the curve increasingly dense. No arrow direction, coordinate label, or filled region is printed. End diagram. In the limit—a notion which had, by now, received rigorous definition—the entire square is filled in solid red. And, in passing, Hilbert's curve is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere; intuitively because, in the infinite limit, the function abruptly changes direction at every moment. (We will outline Hilbert's construction in more detail in the appendix on Hilbert's space-filling curves .) For better or worse, these “pathological” geometric constructions were treated as a reason to doubt appeals to geometric intuition. They became something approaching propaganda for a new way of doing mathematics, which would culminate in set theory. In the later myth-building of the subject, it was repeated, often, that these results were both perfectly rigorous and perfectly shocking. They therefore served a dual purpose: as a warning against relying upon geometric intuition, and as a demonstration of the fertility of new ways of thinking. End section.

listen_text: Section. More Myth than History?. Looking back on these events with more than a century of hindsight, we must be careful not to take these verdicts on trust. The results were certainly novel, exciting, and surprising. But how truly shocking were they? And did they really demonstrate that we should not rely on geometric intuition? On the question of shock, Fernando Gouvea's account Was Cantor Surprised points out that Cantor's famous note to Dedekind, “ je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas ” is taken rather out of context. Here is more of that context (quoted from Fernando Gouvea ): Quotation. Please excuse my zeal for the subject if I make so many demands upon your kindness and patience; the communications which I lately sent you are even for me so unexpected, so new, that I can have no peace of mind until I obtain from you, honoured friend, a decision about their correctness. So long as you have not agreed with me, I can only say: je le vois, mais je ne le crois pas. End quotation. Cantor knew his result was “so unexpected, so new”. But it is doubtful that he ever found his result unbelievable. As Fernando Gouvea points out, he was simply asking Dedekind to check the proof he had offered. On the question of geometric intuition: Peano published his space-filling curve without including any diagrams. But when Hilbert published his curve, he explained his purpose: he would provide readers with a clear way to understand Peano's result, if they “help themselves to the following geometric intuition”; whereupon he included a series of diagrams just like those provided in the section Pathologies . More generally: whilst diagrams have fallen rather out of fashion in published proofs, there is no getting round the fact that mathematicians frequently use diagrams when proving things. (Roughly put: good mathematicians know when they can rely upon geometric intuition.) In short: don't believe the hype; or at least, don't just take it on trust. For more on this, you could read Marcus Giaquinto's book Visual Thinking in Mathematics . End section.

(Roughly put: good mathematicians know when they can rely upon geometric intuition.) In short: don't believe the hype; or at least, don't just take it on trust. For more on this, you could read Marcus Giaquinto's book Visual Thinking in Mathematics . End section.

listen_text: Section. Cantor on the Line and the Plane. Some of the circumstances surrounding the proof of Schroeder-Bernstein tie in with the history we discussed in the section Pathologies . Recall that, in one thousand eight hundred seventy seven, Cantor proved that there are exactly as many points on a square as on one of its sides. Here, we will present his (first attempted) proof. Let the unit interval be the unit line, that is, the set of points the closed interval from zero to one . Let the unit square be the unit square, that is, the set of points the Cartesian product of the unit interval with itself . In these terms, Cantor proved that the unit interval and the unit square have the same cardinality . He wrote a note to Dedekind, essentially containing the following argument. Theorem. the unit interval and the unit square have the same cardinality End theorem. Proof. Proof: first part.. Fix a and b belong to the unit interval . Write them in binary notation, so that we have infinite sequences of zero s and one s, a sub one , a sub two , and so on, and b sub one , b sub two , and so on, such that: Displayed expression. a has binary expansion zero point a sub one, a sub two, a sub three, a sub four, and so on; b has binary expansion zero point b sub one, b sub two, b sub three, b sub four, and so on; now consider the function f from the unit square to the unit interval, where f of a comma b interleaves the digits as zero point a sub one, b sub one, a sub two, b sub two, a sub three, b sub three, a sub four, b sub four, and so on. End displayed expression. Now f is an injection, since if f of a comma b equals f of c comma d , then a sub n equals c sub n and b sub n equals d sub n for all n is a natural number , so that a equals c and b equals d . End proof. Unfortunately, as Dedekind pointed out to Cantor, this does not answer the original question. Consider binary zero point one zero recurring equals binary zero point one zero one zero one zero one zero one zero and so on . We need that f of a comma b equals binary zero point one zero recurring , where: Displayed expression. a equals binary zero point one recurring, which is binary zero point one one one one one one and so on; b equals zero. End displayed expression. But a equals binary zero point one recurring, which equals one . So, when we say “write a and b in binary notation”, we have to choose which notation to use; and, since f is to be a function, we can use only one of the two possible notations. But if, for example, we use the simple notation, and write a as “ binary one point zero zero zero and so on ”, then we have no pair the ordered pair a comma b such that f of a comma b equals binary zero point one zero recurring . To summarise: Dedekind pointed out that, given the possibility of certain recurring decimal expansions, Cantor's function f is an injection but not a surjection. So Cantor has shown only that the cardinality of the unit square is at most the cardinality of the unit interval and not that the unit square and the unit interval have the same cardinality . Cantor wrote back to Dedekind almost immediately, essentially suggesting that the proof could be completed as follows: Proof. Proof: completed.. So, we have shown that the cardinality of the unit square is at most the cardinality of the unit interval . But there is obviously an injection from the unit interval to the unit square : just lay the line flat along one side of the square. So the cardinality of the unit interval is at most the cardinality of the unit square and the cardinality of the unit square is at most the cardinality of the unit interval . By Schroeder—Bernstein ( the Schroeder-Bernstein theorem ), the unit interval and the unit square have the same cardinality . End proof. But of course, Cantor could not complete the last line in these terms, for the Schroeder-Bernstein Theorem was not yet proved. Indeed, although Cantor would subsequently formulate this as a general conjecture, it was not satisfactorily proved until one thousand eight hundred ninety seven. (And so, later in one thousand eight hundred seventy seven, Cantor offered a different proof of the theorem that the unit interval and unit square have equal cardinality , which did not go via Schroeder—Bernstein.) listen_text: Section. Appendix: Hilbert's Space-filling Curves. In chapter the section Pathologies , we mentioned that Cantor's proof that a line and a square have exactly the same number of points ( the theorem that the unit interval and unit square have equal cardinality ) prompted Peano to ask whether there might be a space-filling curve. He obtained a positive answer in one thousand eight hundred ninety. In this section, we explain (in a hand-wavy way) how to construct Hilbert's space-filling curve (with a tiny tweak). Footnote. For a more rigorous explanation, see Daniel Rose's rigorous explanation of Hilbert's space-filling curve . The tweak amounts to the inclusion of the red parts of the curves below. This makes it slightly easier to check that the curve is continuous. End footnote. We must define a function, h , as the limit of a sequence of functions h sub one , h sub two , h sub three , and so on We first describe the construction. Then we show it is space-filling. Then we show it is a curve. We will take h apostrophe s range to be the unit square, the unit square . Here is our first approximation to h , that is, h sub one : First Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by a two by two grid. A black first-order Hilbert path connects the four quarter-cells in the order bottom left, top left, top right, bottom right. Short red segments connect the two bottom endpoints to the square boundary. End diagram. To keep track of things, we have imposed a two by two grid on the square. We can think of the curve starting in the bottom left quarter, moving to the top left, then to the top right, then finally to the bottom right. Here is the second stage in the construction, that is, h sub two : Second Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by a four by four grid. Four scaled black copies of the first-order core occupy the quarter-squares. The lower-left copy is rotated two hundred seventy degrees, the two upper copies are unrotated, and the lower-right copy is rotated ninety degrees. Three green segments join consecutive copies, and two red segments connect the outer endpoints to the left and right boundary. End diagram. The different colours will help explain how h sub two was constructed. We first place scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub one into the bottom left, top left, top right, and bottom right of our square (drawn in black). We then connect these four figures (with green lines). Finally, we connect our figure to the boundary of the square (with red lines). Now to h sub three . Just as h sub two was made from four connected, scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub one , so h sub three is made up of four scaled-down copies of the non-red bit of h sub two (drawn in black), which are then joined together (with green lines) and finally connected to the boundary of the square (with red lines). Third Hilbert-curve approximation in a square divided by an eight by eight grid. Four scaled black copies of the second-order core occupy the quarter-squares. The lower-left copy is rotated two hundred seventy degrees, the two upper copies are unrotated, and the lower-right copy is rotated ninety degrees. The source draws three distinct green connector positions, but repeats the right connector command once at the same coordinates; two red segments connect the outer endpoints to the bottom boundary. End diagram. And now we see the general pattern for defining h sub n plus one from h sub n . At last we define the curve h itself by considering the point-by-point limit of these successive functions h sub one , h sub two , and so on That is, for each x is a point of the unit square : Displayed expression. h of x equals the limit, as n tends to infinity, of h sub n of x. End displayed expression. We now show that this curve fills space. When we draw the curve h sub n , we impose a two to the n by two to the n grid onto the unit square . By Pythagoras's Theorem, the diagonal of each grid-location is of length: Displayed expression. the square root of the sum of two copies of one over two to the n, squared, equals two to the power one half minus n. End displayed expression. and evidently h sub n passes through every grid-location. So each point in the unit square is at most two to the power one half minus n distance away from some point on h sub n . Now, h is defined as the limit of the functions h sub one , h sub two , h sub three , and so on So the maximum distance of any point from h is given by: Displayed expression. the limit, as n tends to infinity, of two to the power one half minus n, equals zero. End displayed expression. That is: every point in the unit square is zero distance from h . In other words, every point of the unit square lies on the curve. So h fills space! Source anomaly note. Source diagram note. The right green connector of the third approximation is drawn twice at identical coordinates. It is one visible segment; both source commands are preserved in the structural account. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. It remains to show that h is, indeed, a curve. To show this, we must define the notion. The modern definition builds on one given by Jordan in one thousand eight hundred eighty seven (that is, only a few years before the first space-filling curve was provided): Definition. A curve is a continuous map from the unit interval to the real plane . End definition. This is fairly intuitive: a curve is, intuitively, a “smooth” map which takes a canonical line onto the plane the real plane . Our function, h , is indeed a map from the unit interval to the real plane . So, we just need to show that h is continuous. We defined continuity in the section Rigorous Definition of Limits using epsilon slash delta notation. In the vernacular, we want to establish the following: If you specify a point p in the unit square , together with any desired level of precision epsilon , we can find an open section of the unit interval such that, given any x in that open section, h of x is within epsilon of p . So: assume that you have specified p and epsilon . This is, in effect, to draw a circle with centre p and radius epsilon on the unit square . (The circle might spill off the edge of the unit square , but that doesn't matter.) Now, recall that, when describing the function h sub n , we drew a two to the n by two to the n grid upon the unit square . It is obvious that, no matter how small epsilon is, there is some n such that some individual grid-location of the two to the n by two to the n grid on the unit square lies wholly within the circle with centre p and radius epsilon . So, take that n , and let the open interval I be the largest open part of the unit interval which h sub n maps wholly into the relevant grid location. (It is clear that the open interval from a to b exists, since we already noted that h sub n passes through every grid-location in the two to the n by two to the n grid.) It now suffices to show to show that, whenever x belongs to the open interval I the point h of x lies in that same grid-location. And to do this, it suffices to show that h sub m of x lies in that same grid location, for any m is greater than n . But this is obvious. If we consider what happens with h sub m for m is greater than n , we see that exactly the “same part” of the unit interval is mapped into the same grid-location; we just map it into that region in an increasingly stretched-out, wiggly fashion.
